name: chemistry_set4_p1
label: Chemistry: set 4 (organic, environmental and practical chemistry)

papers.title: Introduction to Organic Chemistry: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on introduction to organic chemistry, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The functional group of the alkanols is
questions.explanation:
The hydroxyl group, –OH, gives alkanols such as ethanol, C₂H₅OH, their typical reactions.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- –COOH: –COOH is the carboxyl group of the alkanoic acids.
- –COO–: –COO– is the ester group of the alkanoates.
- C=C: C=C is the functional group of the alkenes.

questions.stem: Which statement about the members of a homologous series is correct?
questions.explanation:
A homologous series has one general formula and functional group; members differ by CH₂ (Mᵣ 14).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- They all have the same physical properties: Physical properties change gradually along the series.
- They all have the same molecular formula: Compounds with the same molecular formula are isomers.
- They have different general formulas: All members share one general formula.

options.label: A
options.content: They all have the same physical properties

options.label: B
options.content: They all have the same molecular formula

options.label: D
options.content: Successive members differ by a CH₂ group

questions.stem: How many structural isomers have the molecular formula C₄H₁₀?
questions.explanation:
C₄H₁₀ has two isomers: butane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃, and 2-methylpropane, CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1: There is also a branched chain: 2-methylpropane.
- 3: Three isomers belong to C₅H₁₂, not C₄H₁₀.
- 4: Numbering the same chain from different ends does not give new compounds.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃?
questions.explanation:
The longest chain is three carbons (propane) with a methyl branch on carbon 2.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- butane: Butane is the straight-chain isomer; this one is branched.
- 1-methylpropane: A methyl group on carbon 1 would just lengthen the chain to butane.
- 2-methylbutane: The longest chain has three carbons, not four.

questions.stem: An organic compound is heated with dry copper(II) oxide. The gas given off turns lime water milky. This shows the presence of
questions.explanation:
Carbon is oxidised by CuO to carbon(IV) oxide, which turns lime water milky.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- hydrogen: Hydrogen forms water, shown by anhydrous copper(II) sulphate turning blue.
- oxygen: This test does not detect oxygen in the compound.
- nitrogen: Nitrogen is not detected by lime water.

papers.title: Alkanes: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on alkanes, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The general formula of the alkanes is
questions.explanation:
Methane CH₄ (n = 1), ethane C₂H₆ (n = 2), propane C₃H₈ (n = 3) all fit CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- CₙH₂ₙ: CₙH₂ₙ is the general formula of the alkenes.
- CₙH₂ₙ₋₂: CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ is the general formula of the alkynes.
- CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH: CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH is the general formula of the alkanols.

questions.stem: An alkane has a relative molecular mass of 72. What is its molecular formula?
questions.explanation:
For CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, Mᵣ = 14n + 2 = 72, so n = 5: C₅H₁₂ (pentane).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- C₆H₁₄: C₆H₁₄ has Mᵣ 86.
- C₅H₁₀: C₅H₁₀ (Mᵣ 70) is an alkene, not an alkane.
- C₄H₁₀: C₄H₁₀ has Mᵣ 58.

questions.stem: Methane reacts with chlorine in sunlight to form chloromethane and hydrogen chloride. This is
questions.explanation:
CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl: a chlorine atom replaces (substitutes) a hydrogen atom.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- an addition reaction: Methane has no double bond to add across.
- a polymerisation reaction: No long chains are formed.
- a neutralisation reaction: No acid reacts with a base.

questions.stem: Methane is prepared in the laboratory by heating
questions.explanation:
CH₃COONa + NaOH → CH₄ + Na₂CO₃; the methane is collected over water.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- ethanol with concentrated sulphuric acid: That prepares ethene.
- calcium carbide with water: That prepares ethyne (and needs no heating).
- ethanol with acidified potassium dichromate(VI): That oxidises ethanol to ethanal and ethanoic acid.

questions.stem: 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O. What volume of oxygen is needed to burn 20 cm³ of ethane completely (same conditions)?
questions.explanation:
Volume of O₂ $= 20 \times \dfrac{7}{2} = 70$ cm³

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 140 cm³: You multiplied by 7 without dividing by 2; the ratio is 2 : 7.
- 40 cm³: That is the volume of carbon(IV) oxide formed.
- 20 cm³: You assumed a 1 : 1 ratio.

papers.title: Alkenes: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on alkenes, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which test distinguishes ethene from ethane?
questions.explanation:
The C=C bond in ethene adds bromine at once (CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br); ethane is saturated.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Ethene turns lime water milky; ethane does not: Neither gas turns lime water milky.
- Ethene relights a glowing splint; ethane does not: Neither gas relights a glowing splint.
- Ethene turns damp red litmus blue; ethane does not: Neither gas is alkaline.

options.label: A
options.content: Ethene decolourises bromine water quickly; ethane does not

options.label: B
options.content: Ethene turns lime water milky; ethane does not

options.label: C
options.content: Ethene relights a glowing splint; ethane does not

options.label: D
options.content: Ethene turns damp red litmus blue; ethane does not

questions.stem: Ethene is prepared in the laboratory by heating ethanol with
questions.explanation:
C₂H₅OH → C₂H₄ + H₂O: the acid is a dehydrating agent. At 140 °C ethoxyethane forms instead.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- soda lime: Soda lime with sodium ethanoate gives methane.
- water and calcium carbide: That gives ethyne.
- acidified potassium dichromate(VI): That oxidises ethanol; it does not give ethene.

options.label: C
options.content: excess concentrated sulphuric acid at about 170 °C

questions.stem: The catalyst used when hydrogen is added to ethene (or to vegetable oils) is
questions.explanation:
CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃CH₃ over finely divided nickel at about 150 °C; the same reaction makes margarine.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- iron: Iron is the catalyst in the Haber process.
- vanadium(V) oxide: Vanadium(V) oxide is used in the Contact process.
- manganese(IV) oxide: Manganese(IV) oxide catalyses the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.

questions.stem: What is the main product when hydrogen bromide adds to propene, CH₃CH=CH₂?
questions.explanation:
By Markovnikov's rule, the H of HBr goes to the CH₂ end and Br to the middle carbon: 2-bromopropane.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- CH₃CH₂CH₂Br: This is the minor product; H adds to the carbon that already has more hydrogens.
- CH₂BrCHBrCH₃: That would be the product of adding Br₂, not HBr.
- CH₃CH=CHBr: Addition removes the double bond; this still has one.

questions.stem: What mass of bromine, Br₂, adds to 2.8 g of ethene? CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br (C₂H₄ = 28; Br₂ = 160)
questions.explanation:
Moles C₂H₄ $= \dfrac{2.8}{28} = 0.1$; moles Br₂ $= 0.1$; mass $= 0.1 \times 160 = 16$ g

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 32 g: One C=C bond adds one molecule of Br₂, not two.
- 8 g: You used 80 (one Br atom) as the molar mass of bromine.
- 18.8 g: That is the mass of the product, 1,2-dibromoethane.

papers.title: Alkynes: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on alkynes, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Ethyne is prepared in the laboratory by the action of water on
questions.explanation:
CaC₂ + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + C₂H₂. Water is dripped onto the carbide because the reaction is vigorous.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- calcium carbonate: Calcium carbonate does not react with water.
- sodium ethanoate: Sodium ethanoate heated with soda lime gives methane.
- ethanol: Water does not react with ethanol to give a gas.

questions.stem: The shape of the ethyne molecule, HC≡CH, is
questions.explanation:
Each carbon forms a triple bond and one C–H bond, all in a straight line.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- tetrahedral, with bond angles of 109.5°: That is the shape around each carbon in ethane.
- planar, with bond angles of 120°: That is the shape of ethene.
- bent, with bond angles of 104.5°: That is the shape of the water molecule.

questions.stem: Which reagent gives a precipitate with ethyne but not with ethene?
questions.explanation:
The H atoms on the C≡C are weakly acidic: ethyne gives a white precipitate of silver dicarbide, Ag₂C₂.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Bromine water: Both ethene and ethyne decolourise bromine water.
- Acidified potassium manganate(VII): Both unsaturated gases decolourise it.
- Lime water: Neither gas reacts with lime water.

questions.stem: What volume of hydrogen is needed to convert 50 cm³ of ethyne completely into ethane (same conditions)? C₂H₂ + 2H₂ → C₂H₆
questions.explanation:
1 volume of ethyne needs 2 volumes of hydrogen: $2 \times 50 = 100$ cm³

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 50 cm³: That converts ethyne only to ethene; two molecules of H₂ are needed to reach ethane.
- 25 cm³: You halved instead of doubling.
- 150 cm³: Ethyne adds two molecules of hydrogen, not three.

questions.stem: Ethyne burned in pure oxygen is used for
questions.explanation:
The oxy-acetylene flame reaches about 3000 °C, hot enough to melt steel.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- making plastic bags: Plastic bags are made from poly(ethene).
- ripening fruit safely: Calcium carbide (which gives ethyne) is misused for ripening; it is unsafe.
- filling light bulbs: Light bulbs are filled with argon.

papers.title: Petroleum and Petrochemicals: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on petroleum and petrochemicals, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Crude oil is separated into fractions by fractional distillation because its components have different
questions.explanation:
Each fraction condenses at the level of the column where the temperature falls below its boiling point.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- densities: Separation in the column depends on boiling point, not density.
- colours: Colour plays no part in the separation.
- solubilities in water: Hydrocarbons are almost insoluble in water; water is not used.

questions.stem: Which petroleum fraction is used as fuel for jet aircraft?
questions.explanation:
Kerosene (about C₁₀–C₁₆) is used as aviation fuel and in lamps and stoves.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Bitumen: Bitumen is used for road surfaces.
- Lubricating oil: Lubricating oil reduces friction in engines.
- Refinery gas: Refinery gas is used as LPG for cooking.

questions.stem: Cracking is the process of
questions.explanation:
Cracking uses heat and often a catalyst (Al₂O₃/SiO₂); it gives smaller alkanes and alkenes such as ethene.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- separating crude oil into fractions: That is fractional distillation.
- joining small molecules into polymers: That is polymerisation.
- removing sulphur from crude oil: That is desulphurisation.

options.label: A
options.content: breaking large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more useful ones

questions.stem: Petrol with a high octane number contains a high proportion of
questions.explanation:
2,2,4-trimethylpentane (octane number 100) is branched; heptane (0) is a straight chain.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- straight-chain alkanes: Straight chains knock easily and have low octane numbers.
- water: Water is an impurity, not a component that raises octane number.
- bitumen: Bitumen is far too heavy to be in petrol.

questions.stem: In the cracking reaction C₁₂H₂₆ → C₈H₁₈ + 2X, what is X?
questions.explanation:
Carbon: 12 − 8 = 4 = 2 × 2; hydrogen: 26 − 18 = 8 = 2 × 4. So X = C₂H₄ (ethene).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- C₄H₈: C₄H₈ would balance 1X, but the equation shows 2X.
- C₂H₆: Two C₂H₆ would need 12 more H atoms than are available.
- C₄H₁₀: This does not balance carbon or hydrogen with 2X.

papers.title: Alkanols: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on alkanols, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The enzyme in yeast that converts glucose into ethanol and carbon(IV) oxide is
questions.explanation:
C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂, catalysed by zymase at about 25–35 °C without air.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- diastase: Diastase (in malt) converts starch into maltose.
- maltase: Maltase converts maltose into glucose.
- amylase: Amylase (in saliva) converts starch into maltose.

questions.stem: Propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃, is classified as
questions.explanation:
The carbon carrying –OH is joined to two other carbon atoms, so propan-2-ol is secondary.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a primary alkanol: In a primary alkanol, the C–OH carbon is joined to only one other carbon.
- a tertiary alkanol: In a tertiary alkanol, the C–OH carbon is joined to three other carbons.
- a dihydric alkanol: It has only one –OH group.

questions.stem: When ethanol is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate(VI), the colour changes from
questions.explanation:
Ethanol is oxidised to ethanal and then ethanoic acid; Cr₂O₇²⁻ is reduced to Cr³⁺.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- purple to colourless: That is the change with acidified potassium manganate(VII).
- green to orange: Dichromate(VI) is orange; it is reduced to green Cr³⁺.
- colourless to pink: That is phenolphthalein turning alkaline.

questions.stem: What mass of ethanol is formed by the complete fermentation of 18 g of glucose? C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ (C₆H₁₂O₆ = 180; C₂H₅OH = 46)
questions.explanation:
Moles glucose $= \dfrac{18}{180} = 0.1$; moles ethanol $= 0.2$; mass $= 0.2 \times 46 = 9.2$ g

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 4.6 g: You used a 1 : 1 ratio; each glucose gives two ethanol molecules.
- 8.8 g: That is the mass of carbon(IV) oxide formed.
- 18 g: Some of the mass is lost as carbon(IV) oxide.

questions.stem: Sodium reacts with ethanol to give
questions.explanation:
2C₂H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂. The fizzing is a test for an –OH group.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- sodium hydroxide and hydrogen: That is the product with water, not ethanol.
- sodium ethanoate and water: Sodium ethanoate forms from ethanoic acid and sodium hydroxide.
- ethene and sodium hydroxide: Sodium does not dehydrate ethanol.

papers.title: Alkanoic Acids: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on alkanoic acids, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The functional group of the alkanoic acids is
questions.explanation:
The carboxyl group, –COOH, contains a C=O and an –OH on the same carbon.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- –OH: –OH is the hydroxyl group of the alkanols.
- –CHO: –CHO is the aldehyde (alkanal) group.
- –NH₂: –NH₂ is the amino group.

questions.stem: Which reagent distinguishes ethanoic acid from ethanol?
questions.explanation:
Ethanoic acid gives effervescence of CO₂ with NaHCO₃; ethanol does not react.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Sodium metal: Both compounds fizz with sodium, giving hydrogen.
- Water: Both are miscible with water.
- A lighted splint held over the liquid: Both are flammable liquids; this is not a safe or clear test.

options.label: D
options.content: A lighted splint held over the liquid

questions.stem: The IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂COOH is
questions.explanation:
Count all the carbons including the one in –COOH: three, so propanoic acid.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- ethanoic acid: The carbon of –COOH is counted: there are three carbons.
- propan-1-ol: Propan-1-ol is an alkanol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH.
- butanoic acid: Butanoic acid has four carbons, C₃H₇COOH.

questions.stem: A vinegar contains 0.80 mol/dm³ of ethanoic acid. What is its concentration in g/dm³? (CH₃COOH = 60)
questions.explanation:
Mass concentration $= 0.80 \times 60 = 48$ g/dm³

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.013 g/dm³: You divided the concentration by the molar mass.
- 75 g/dm³: You divided the molar mass by the concentration.
- 36.8 g/dm³: You used 46, the molar mass of ethanol.

questions.stem: Compared with 0.1 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid, 0.1 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid
questions.explanation:
Ethanoic acid is only partly ionised; its pH is about 3, while that of 0.1 mol/dm³ HCl is 1.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- has a lower pH: Ethanoic acid is weak and produces fewer H⁺ ions, so its pH is higher.
- neutralises more sodium hydroxide: Equal volumes neutralise the same amount of NaOH (both are monobasic).
- conducts electricity better: It has fewer ions, so it conducts less well.

papers.title: Alkanoates and Esters: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on alkanoates and esters, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The name of the ester CH₃COOC₂H₅ is
questions.explanation:
The alkanol part (C₂H₅–, ethyl) is named first, then the acid part (CH₃COO–, ethanoate).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- methyl propanoate: That is CH₃CH₂COOCH₃.
- ethyl methanoate: That is HCOOC₂H₅.
- propyl methanoate: That is HCOOC₃H₇.

questions.stem: In the preparation of an ester from an alkanoic acid and an alkanol, concentrated sulphuric acid acts as
questions.explanation:
It speeds up the reaction and absorbs the water formed, shifting the equilibrium towards the ester.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- an oxidising agent: Nothing is oxidised in esterification.
- a reducing agent: Concentrated sulphuric acid is not a reducing agent.
- the source of the ester group: The ester group comes from the acid and the alkanol.

options.label: A
options.content: a catalyst and a dehydrating agent

options.label: D
options.content: the source of the ester group

questions.stem: Which property is typical of simple esters such as ethyl ethanoate?
questions.explanation:
Esters are volatile, pleasant-smelling and used as flavourings, perfumes and solvents.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- A sharp smell of vinegar and solubility in water: That describes ethanoic acid.
- Effervescence with sodium carbonate: Esters are neutral; only acids fizz with carbonates.
- A high boiling point due to hydrogen bonding: Esters cannot hydrogen-bond with each other, so their boiling points are low.

options.label: A
options.content: A sharp smell of vinegar and solubility in water

options.label: B
options.content: A sweet, fruity smell and insolubility in water

options.label: D
options.content: A high boiling point due to hydrogen bonding

questions.stem: 12 g of ethanoic acid is warmed with excess ethanol and gives 11.44 g of ethyl ethanoate. What is the percentage yield? (CH₃COOH = 60; CH₃COOC₂H₅ = 88)
questions.explanation:
Moles acid $= \dfrac{12}{60} = 0.2$; theoretical ester $= 0.2 \times 88 = 17.6$ g; yield $= \dfrac{11.44}{17.6} \times 100 = 65\%$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 95.33%: You compared the mass of ester with the mass of acid used.
- 35%: That is the percentage that was not obtained.
- 153.85%: You divided the theoretical mass by the actual mass.

questions.stem: Which compound is a functional group isomer of propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH?
questions.explanation:
Both are C₃H₆O₂, but one is an acid (–COOH) and the other an ester (–COO–).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH: Propan-1-ol is C₃H₈O; propanoic acid is C₃H₆O₂.
- Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH: Ethanoic acid is C₂H₄O₂, a different formula.
- Propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO: Propanal is C₃H₆O.

papers.title: Soaps, Detergents, and Oils: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on soaps, detergents, and oils, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: When a fat is boiled with sodium hydroxide solution, the products are
questions.explanation:
Saponification: fat + 3NaOH → glycerol + 3 sodium salts of fatty acids (soap).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- soap and ethanol: The alkanol released from fats is glycerol, not ethanol.
- margarine and water: Margarine is made by hydrogenating oils.
- glycerol and fatty acids only: In alkali, the fatty acids form their sodium salts (soap).

questions.stem: In soap making, the soap is separated from the glycerol solution by adding
questions.explanation:
Salting out: soap is much less soluble in brine, so it separates as a curd that floats.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- sodium hydroxide: Sodium hydroxide is the alkali used to saponify the fat.
- calcium chloride: Calcium ions would form insoluble scum, spoiling the soap.
- ethanol: Ethanol would dissolve the soap rather than separate it.

questions.stem: Soap forms a scum in hard water because
questions.explanation:
2C₁₇H₃₅COO⁻ + Ca²⁺ → (C₁₇H₃₅COO)₂Ca(s). Soapless detergents do not form scum.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- hard water is too acidic: Hardness is caused by Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions, not acidity.
- soap does not dissolve in water: Soap dissolves in soft water and lathers well.
- hard water contains chloride ions: Chloride ions do not react with soap.

options.label: B
options.content: calcium and magnesium ions form insoluble salts with the soap

options.label: C
options.content: soap does not dissolve in water

questions.stem: Vegetable oils are liquid at room temperature while animal fats are solid because oils contain
questions.explanation:
Kinks at C=C bonds stop the chains packing closely, so the forces between molecules are weaker.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- more saturated fatty acid chains: Saturated chains pack closely and make fats solid.
- no glycerol: Both fats and oils are esters of glycerol.
- water: Oils are not liquid because of water.

questions.stem: Which part of a soap anion dissolves in grease?
questions.explanation:
The hydrophobic tail dissolves in the grease and the ionic head stays in the water, lifting the grease off.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- The –COO⁻ group: The ionic head is hydrophilic and dissolves in water.
- The sodium ion: Na⁺ is separate from the anion and stays in the water.
- The whole anion equally: The two ends behave differently; that is how soap works.

papers.title: Carbohydrates: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on carbohydrates, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Starch gives a blue-black colour with
questions.explanation:
Iodine forms a blue-black complex with starch; it stays brown-yellow with sugars.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Benedict's solution: Benedict's solution tests for reducing sugars.
- biuret reagent: The biuret test detects proteins.
- bromine water: Bromine water tests for C=C bonds.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a reducing sugar?
questions.explanation:
Sucrose gives no precipitate with Benedict's solution until it is hydrolysed to glucose and fructose.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Glucose: Glucose gives a brick-red precipitate with Benedict's solution.
- Fructose: Fructose is a reducing sugar.
- Maltose: Maltose is a reducing sugar.

questions.stem: The products of the acid hydrolysis of sucrose are
questions.explanation:
C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose) + C₆H₁₂O₆ (fructose).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- glucose only: Maltose, not sucrose, gives glucose only.
- glucose and galactose: Lactose gives glucose and galactose.
- ethanol and carbon(IV) oxide: Those are products of fermentation.

questions.stem: What mass of glucose is produced by the complete hydrolysis of 342 g of sucrose? C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + C₆H₁₂O₆ (sucrose = 342; glucose = 180)
questions.explanation:
Moles sucrose $= \dfrac{342}{342} = 1$; it gives 1 mol glucose $= 180$ g (and 1 mol fructose).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 360 g: Sucrose gives one glucose and one fructose, not two glucose.
- 342 g: Mass of sucrose is not the mass of glucose formed.
- 171 g: You halved the mass of sucrose.

questions.stem: The enzyme in saliva that hydrolyses starch is
questions.explanation:
Salivary amylase hydrolyses starch to maltose, which is why bread tastes sweet when chewed.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- zymase: Zymase in yeast ferments glucose to ethanol.
- pepsin: Pepsin hydrolyses proteins in the stomach.
- invertase: Invertase hydrolyses sucrose.

papers.title: Proteins and Amino Acids: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on proteins and amino acids, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which element is present in all proteins but not in carbohydrates?
questions.explanation:
Proteins are built from amino acids, each with an –NH₂ group; carbohydrates contain only C, H and O.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Carbon: Carbohydrates also contain carbon.
- Oxygen: Carbohydrates also contain oxygen.
- Hydrogen: Carbohydrates also contain hydrogen.

questions.stem: The link that joins amino acids together in a protein is
questions.explanation:
The peptide (amide) link forms when –COOH of one amino acid reacts with –NH₂ of the next, losing water.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- –COO–: –COO– is the ester link in fats and polyesters.
- –O–: –O– links sugar units in starch and cellulose.
- –C=C–: C=C is the functional group of alkenes.

questions.stem: A food sample gives a violet colour when sodium hydroxide and a few drops of dilute copper(II) sulphate are added. This shows the presence of
questions.explanation:
This is the biuret test: Cu²⁺ in alkali forms a violet complex with peptide bonds.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- starch: Starch is detected with iodine.
- a reducing sugar: Reducing sugars are detected with Benedict's or Fehling's solution.
- fat: Fats are detected by the grease-spot or emulsion test.

questions.stem: When egg white is heated it becomes a white solid. During this denaturation,
questions.explanation:
Heat breaks the hydrogen bonds that hold the folded shape; the chain unfolds and the protein coagulates.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the protein is hydrolysed to amino acids: Hydrolysis breaks peptide bonds; heating an egg does not.
- new peptide bonds form between the chains: Denaturation does not make new peptide bonds.
- the protein is converted into starch: Proteins do not turn into carbohydrates on heating.

options.label: A
options.content: the protein is hydrolysed to amino acids

options.label: B
options.content: new peptide bonds form between the chains

options.label: C
options.content: the protein is converted into starch

options.label: D
options.content: the 3-D shape of the protein changes but the peptide bonds are not broken

questions.stem: Glycine (Mᵣ = 75) and alanine (Mᵣ = 89) join to form a dipeptide. What is the relative molecular mass of the dipeptide? (H₂O = 18)
questions.explanation:
$M_r = 75 + 89 - 18 = 146$ (one H₂O is eliminated in the condensation).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 164: You forgot that a molecule of water is lost when the peptide bond forms.
- 128: Only one molecule of water is lost, not two.
- 182: Water is lost, not added.

papers.title: Polymers and Plastics: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on polymers and plastics, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The monomer of PVC is
questions.explanation:
n CH₂=CHCl → (–CH₂–CHCl–)ₙ, poly(chloroethene), used for water pipes.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- ethene, CH₂=CH₂: Ethene is the monomer of poly(ethene).
- propene, CH₂=CHCH₃: Propene is the monomer of poly(propene).
- chloroethane, CH₃CH₂Cl: Chloroethane has no C=C bond, so it cannot form an addition polymer.

questions.stem: Nylon is formed by
questions.explanation:
A diamine and a dicarboxylic acid join through amide links, losing water at each link.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- addition polymerisation: Addition polymers form from C=C monomers with no by-product.
- fermentation: Fermentation produces ethanol from sugars.
- cracking: Cracking breaks large molecules into smaller ones.

questions.stem: A thermosetting plastic does not soften on heating because
questions.explanation:
Covalent cross-links stop the chains sliding past each other, so the plastic chars rather than melts.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- its chains are short: Thermosets have long chains, joined to each other.
- it contains no carbon: Thermosetting plastics are organic polymers.
- it is held together only by weak forces: Weak forces between chains allow a thermoplastic to soften.

options.label: C
options.content: its chains are joined by strong cross-links

options.label: D
options.content: it is held together only by weak forces

questions.stem: A sample of poly(ethene) has a relative molecular mass of 42 000. How many ethene units does each chain contain? (C₂H₄ = 28)
questions.explanation:
$n = \dfrac{M_r(\text{polymer})}{M_r(\text{monomer})} = \dfrac{42\,000}{28} = 1500$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 3000: You used 14 (CH₂) as the mass of the monomer; the monomer is C₂H₄.
- 750: You used 56 as the molar mass of ethene.
- 42,000: That is the relative molecular mass, not the number of units.

questions.stem: Vulcanisation of rubber involves heating it with
questions.explanation:
Sulphur forms –S–S– cross-links between the chains, making rubber harder, stronger and more elastic.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- chlorine: Chlorine does not form cross-links in natural rubber.
- nitrogen: Nitrogen is unreactive and is not used.
- carbon(IV) oxide: Carbon(IV) oxide does not react with rubber.

papers.title: Chemistry and the Environment: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on chemistry and the environment, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which gas is the main cause of acid rain from burning coal and fuel oil?
questions.explanation:
SO₂ dissolves in rain and is oxidised to sulphuric(VI) acid: 2SO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 2H₂SO₄.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Carbon(II) oxide: Carbon(II) oxide is poisonous but does not form acid rain.
- Methane: Methane is a greenhouse gas, not a cause of acid rain.
- Nitrogen: Nitrogen gas itself is unreactive; its oxides (NOₓ) contribute.

questions.stem: The burning of fossil fuels adds most to global warming by increasing the amount of which gas in the air?
questions.explanation:
CO₂ absorbs infrared radiation from the Earth and re-emits it, trapping heat (the greenhouse effect).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Oxygen: Burning uses up oxygen; it does not add it.
- Nitrogen: Nitrogen is not a greenhouse gas.
- Argon: Argon is not produced by burning and is not a greenhouse gas.

questions.stem: Carbon(II) oxide from a generator running in a closed room is dangerous because it
questions.explanation:
CO binds about 200 times more strongly than oxygen to haemoglobin, causing drowsiness and death.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- causes acid rain: Carbon(II) oxide does not form acid rain.
- destroys the ozone layer: CFCs destroy ozone.
- has a strong choking smell that damages the lungs: Carbon(II) oxide is odourless, which makes it more dangerous.

options.label: C
options.content: combines with haemoglobin and stops the blood carrying oxygen

options.label: D
options.content: has a strong choking smell that damages the lungs

questions.stem: Eutrophication of a lake is caused mainly by
questions.explanation:
Nutrients cause algal blooms; when the algae die, bacteria decomposing them use up the dissolved oxygen.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- sulphur(IV) oxide from factories: Sulphur(IV) oxide causes acid rain.
- carbon(IV) oxide from vehicles: Carbon(IV) oxide causes global warming.
- oil spills from ships: Oil spills coat water and wildlife; they do not cause algal blooms.

options.label: D
options.content: nitrates and phosphates from fertilisers and detergents

questions.stem: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) harm the environment mainly by
questions.explanation:
UV light releases chlorine atoms from CFCs; these destroy ozone, letting more harmful UV reach the ground.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- causing acid rain: CFCs do not form acids in rain.
- poisoning fish in rivers: CFCs are not the main river pollutants.
- making water hard: Hardness is caused by calcium and magnesium ions.

options.label: A
options.content: destroying ozone in the upper atmosphere

papers.title: Practical Chemistry Skills: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on practical chemistry skills, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A solution, acidified with dilute hydrochloric acid, gives a white precipitate with barium chloride solution. The anion present is
questions.explanation:
Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄(s), a white precipitate insoluble in acid.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- chloride, Cl⁻: Chloride is tested with acidified silver nitrate.
- carbonate, CO₃²⁻: The acid removes carbonate ions, which fizz instead.
- nitrate, NO₃⁻: Nitrate is tested by the brown-ring test.

questions.stem: Which test shows that a salt contains the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺?
questions.explanation:
NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O on warming; ammonia is the only common alkaline gas.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Adding dilute acid gives a gas that turns lime water milky: That shows a carbonate.
- Adding silver nitrate gives a white precipitate: That shows a chloride.
- A flame test gives a lilac colour: That shows potassium.

options.label: A
options.content: Adding dilute acid gives a gas that turns lime water milky

options.label: B
options.content: Adding silver nitrate gives a white precipitate

options.label: C
options.content: Warming with sodium hydroxide solution gives a gas that turns damp red litmus blue

options.label: D
options.content: A flame test gives a lilac colour

questions.stem: A solution gives a white precipitate with NaOH(aq) that dissolves in excess, and a white precipitate with NH₃(aq) that also dissolves in excess. The cation is
questions.explanation:
Only zinc hydroxide dissolves in excess of both reagents (zincate with NaOH, a complex ion with NH₃).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Al³⁺: Aluminium hydroxide does not dissolve in excess ammonia.
- Pb²⁺: Lead(II) hydroxide does not dissolve in excess ammonia.
- Ca²⁺: Calcium hydroxide does not dissolve in excess NaOH, and ammonia gives no precipitate.

questions.stem: A solution acidified with dilute nitric acid gives a white precipitate with silver nitrate solution, soluble in excess ammonia. The anion present is
questions.explanation:
Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl(s), a white precipitate that dissolves in excess aqueous ammonia.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- iodide, I⁻: Silver iodide is yellow and insoluble in ammonia.
- bromide, Br⁻: Silver bromide is cream and only slightly soluble in ammonia.
- sulphate, SO₄²⁻: Sulphate is tested with acidified barium chloride.

questions.stem: Which burette reading is correctly recorded?
questions.explanation:
A burette is read to ±0.05 cm³, so readings are given to two decimal places with the last digit 0 or 5.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 23.4 cm³: Burette readings are recorded to two decimal places.
- 23 cm³: A whole number loses the precision of the burette.
- 23.405 cm³: A burette cannot be read to three decimal places.
